en: Can a whole group of people evolve to be better at diving?
Most of us struggle to stay underwater for even one minute.
So, yes or no? Take a guess.
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Meet the Bajau, the sea nomads of Southeast Asia.
They live across the islands of Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Many homes stand on stilts right above the water.
There are no streets here. People get around by boat.
Kids learn to swim when they are very young, because the sea is where the food is.
Some Bajau divers spend up to sixty percent of their workday underwater.
With only a simple wooden mask, some go deeper than seventy meters.
They spear fish and crabs, all on a single breath.
And they have lived this way for more than a thousand years.
So scientists checked one organ with ultrasound: the spleen.
On average, Bajau spleens were about fifty percent bigger than those of their neighbors on land.
Why does that matter?
Your spleen stores red blood cells full of oxygen.
When you dive, it squeezes them into your blood, like a spare air tank.
And the team found gene changes that seem to make it bigger.
So yes.
After a thousand years at sea, the Bajau body seems to have adapted for diving.
Stay curious!
